# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXV. ANOTHER SCANDAL AND ANOTHER “EXPLANATION”

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Grace arrived at Sunday School early and sat down in the corner of her class pew before anybody else got there. Consequently, nobody realized the awful truth until Grace walked from the class pew beside the door up to the manse pew when Sunday School ended. The church was half full by that time, and everyone seated beside the aisle noticed that boots were on the minister’s daughter, but she had no stockings!
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0000 }

Aunt Martha had crafted Grace’s new brown dress using an old pattern, rendering it absurdly long for her, yet it still failed to reach her boot-tops. A clear two inches of bare white leg were plainly visible.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0001 }

Grace and Rupert were the sole occupants of the manse pew. Tobias had moved to the gallery so he could sit beside a friend, whereas Ida had been taken by the Carrow girls. It was the custom of the Ashdown children to be “sitting all over the church” like this, a practice that numerous people deemed highly inappropriate. In particular, the gallery—a gathering spot for careless boys who were heard whispering and believed to chew tobacco throughout the service—was considered unsuitable for a child of the manse. Tobias, however, despised the manse pew located at the church’s highest point, directly beneath the gaze of Elder Clow and his household. He fled from that spot every chance he got.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0002 }

Rupert, who was completely engrossed in observing a spider weaving a web by the window, failed to observe Grace’s legs. As she journeyed back to her house beside her father following the church service, he failed to observe them as well. Prior to the arrival of Tobias and Ida, she put on the detested striped stockings, ensuring that none of the residents in the manse were aware of her actions for the moment. However, every other person in Glen St. Agnes was fully aware of the situation. Those rare individuals who had not witnessed it directly were informed shortly after. During the return trip from the church service, no other topic was discussed. Mrs. Hector Twiss remarked that it was merely what she had anticipated, and before long one would observe some of those youths arriving at church devoid of any garments whatsoever. It was resolved by the president of the Ladies’ Aid that she would introduce the issue during the subsequent Aid gathering, proposing that they visit the minister as a group to raise an objection. Miss Winifred declared that, as far as she was concerned, she surrendered. Continuing to fret over the manse fry served no purpose any further. A slight sense of shock was experienced even by Mrs. Dr. Carrow, although she laid the blame for the event entirely upon the forgetfulness of Grace. Because the day was Sunday, Tabitha was unable to start knitting stockings for Grace right away, yet she had a pair cast onto her needles prior to anyone else rising from bed at Hollowmere on the following morning.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0003 }

“Only that old Martha was to blame is all you need to inform me, Mrs. Dr. dear,” she said to Nell. “My guess is that the poor little girl lacked any proper stockings to put on. My guess is that holes were in every pair she owned, just as you are well aware is usually the case. And it is my opinion, Mrs. Dr. dear, that making some for those children would be a finer use of the Ladies’ Aid’s time than arguing about the fresh rug for the pulpit platform. Although I do not belong to the Ladies’ Aid, I will make Grace two pairs of stockings using this lovely black yarn as quickly as my hands can manage, and you can count on that. My feelings will never leave my memory, Mrs. Dr. dear, from the moment I observed a clergyman’s daughter stepping down the aisle of our church without stockings on her feet. Truly, I was at a loss as to where I should turn my eyes.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0004 }

“And yesterday the church was simply packed with Methodists, as well,” moaned Miss Winifred, who had traveled up to the Glen for a bit of shopping and stopped by Hollowmere so she could discuss the matter. “I cannot explain why, but whenever those children from the manse commit a particularly terrible act, the church is bound to be filled with Methodists. Mrs. Deacon Hazard looked as though her eyes were going to pop right out of her head. Upon leaving the church, she remarked, ‘Well, that display was hardly proper. The Presbyterians have my sympathy.’ And we were forced to accept it. One was completely unable to offer any reply.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0005 }

“Had I overheard her, Mrs. Dr. dear, I might have offered a response,” Tabitha remarked with a stern expression. “To begin with, I would have declared my belief that clean, unclad legs were every bit as respectable as garments full of holes. Furthermore, I would have pointed out that the Presbyterians hardly required any sympathy, given that they possessed a minister capable of delivering a sermon while the Methodists lacked one. Mrs. Dr dear, I could have utterly silenced Mrs. Deacon Hazard, and you can be certain of that.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0006 }

“I wish Mr. Ashdown preached a bit less effectively and took somewhat better care of his family,” Miss Winifred replied. “He might at minimum inspect his children prior to their departure for church to ensure their attire was entirely suitable. Trust me, I am weary of offering excuses on his behalf.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0007 }

In the meantime, Fern Hollow was the place where Grace’s soul was undergoing torment. Mary Stubbs had arrived, and, habitually, she was inclined to give a sermon. She made Grace comprehend that she had brought irredeemable dishonor upon herself as well as her father, and that she, Mary Stubbs, had washed her hands of her. “Everybody” was gossiping, and “everybody” uttered the identical sentiment.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0008 }

“I just think that it is impossible for me to spend time with you from now on,” she finished.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0009 }

“So we will be spending time with her,” Bess Carrow exclaimed. Although Bess privately believed that Grace had committed a terrible act, she refused to allow Mary Stubbs to control things so dictatorially. “Furthermore, Miss Stubbs, if you refuse to do so, you don’t need to visit Fern Hollow ever again.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0010 }

Bess and Izzy each wrapped an arm around Grace, staring at Mary with fiercely protective eyes. Mary unexpectedly lost all her composure, collapsing onto a tree stump as tears started to fall.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0011 }

“I want to, truly,” she cried out. “However, staying on good terms with Grace will make folks claim I encouraged her behavior. Indeed, some people are making those claims right this minute. Having those rumors spread about me is something I can’t risk, now that I have a respectable position and am attempting to act like a lady. Besides, even during my wildest times, I never went into church bare-legged. Such an act would never have crossed my mind. Yet that dreadful old Kitty Hector claims Grace changed for the worse after the period I spent at the manse. According to her, Winifred Kerr is going to regret taking me into her home. It truly wounds my feelings. Nevertheless, the person I’m actually concerned about is Mr. Ashdown.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0012 }

“I feel you do not need to be concerned over him,” Izzy stated with contempt. “It is probably not required. At present, Grace darling, cease your weeping and inform us of your reason for doing it.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0013 }

Grace offered a weeping explanation. Her plight drew sympathy from the Carrow girls, and even Mary Stubbs concurred that her situation was difficult. Tobias, however, hit by the news like a bolt of thunder, would not be appeased. Thus, the cryptic clues he had picked up at school earlier that day were finally made clear! Instantly rushing Grace and Ida back to their house, he left the Good-Conduct Club to assemble right away in the cemetery, where they convened to evaluate Grace’s actions.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0014 }

“I fail to perceive how it caused any damage,” Grace stated with defiance. “Hardly any of my legs were visible. It was not incorrect, nor did it injure anyone.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0015 }

“It is going to cause Dad pain. You are aware that it will. You are aware that people place the blame on him every time we perform any strange action.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0016 }

“That hadn't crossed my mind,” Grace mumbled.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0017 }

“That is precisely the problem. You failed to think when you ought to have thought. Our Club exists for that very purpose—to raise us properly and force us to think. Every one of us promised to constantly pause and think prior to acting. Because you failed to do so, Grace, you must receive punishment—and a truly severe one at that. As your penalty, you will have to wear those striped stockings to school for an entire week.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0018 }

“Oh, Tobias, can’t you make it just one day—or perhaps two days? Why must it be an entire week!”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0019 }

“Indeed, an entire week,” uttered relentless Tobias. “It is just—inquire of Kit Carrow whether it is not.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0020 }

Grace was inclined to yield instead of inquiring of Kit Carrow regarding a topic of that nature. It was starting to dawn on her that the transgression she committed was exceedingly disgraceful.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0021 }

“In that case, I will,” she mumbled, somewhat sullenly.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0022 }

“Your punishment is light,” Tobias said with sternness. “And our disciplining of you cannot undo the harm to father, regardless of what we do. It will constantly be viewed as mere trouble-making on your part, and father will be faulted for failing to prevent it. Making everyone understand will be impossible for us.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0023 }

Grace was troubled by this particular side of the matter. While she could endure her own dishonor, the thought of her father being held at fault agonized her. Should the actual circumstances of the situation become known to the public, he would be freed from fault. Yet, in what way was she to reveal them to everyone? Standing up during a church service to clarify the situation, just as she had formerly done, was completely impossible. Mary Stubbs had informed Grace about the way the churchgoers had viewed that spectacle, making her understand that it could not be done again. For three and a half days, Grace agonized over the dilemma. An idea then struck her, which she carried out without delay. That night was passed in the attic, illuminated by a lamp as she wrote feverishly in a notebook, her face red and her eyes gleaming. No better solution existed! She felt so smart for coming up with it! Everything would be corrected and clarified without creating any public outrage. By eleven o’clock, she completed the task to her liking and went quietly downstairs to sleep, feeling utterly exhausted yet thoroughly joyful.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0024 }

Within a handful of days, The Journal, which was the small weekly paper printed in the Glen, appeared as it always did, delivering yet another shock to the Glen. A piece of correspondence bearing the signature “Grace Ashdown” held a conspicuous spot on the first page, reading in this manner:—
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0025 }

“FOR THE ATTENTION OF THOSE AFFECTED:
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0026 }

“My goal is to make it clear to everyone why I ended up attending church bare-legged, which will prove that father does not deserve a single bit of fault, so those old gossips can stop making that untrue claim. After seeing Zilla Marsh barefoot with her poor little feet freezing, I felt so much pity that I handed over my sole pair of black stockings to her. In a Christian town, no kid should be forced to walk around lacking shoes and stockings until the snow has completely melted, so my opinion is that her stockings should have come from the W. F. M. S. naturally, sending supplies to the young heathen kids is fine and thoughtful, as I well understand. Nevertheless, those young heathen kids enjoy a great deal more warm weather than our climate offers, so Zilla ought to be cared for by the females of our congregation instead of putting everything on my shoulders. It slipped my mind when handing over my stockings that no other holeless black pair remained in my possession, yet making that gift makes me happy, since my conscience would plague me if I had withheld them. Following the departure of the poor little creature, who left filled with pride and joy, it struck me that my only remaining option was to put on those awful red and blue items Aunt Martha created for me previous winter using yarn that arrived from Mrs. Joseph Burr of Upper Glen. That yarn had terrible coarseness and constant knots, and none of Mrs. Burr’s own offspring were ever spotted by me in garments knitted from it. Mary Stubbs claims, however, that Mrs. Burr passes off unusable or inedible items to the minister, believing such offerings should count toward the salary pledged by her husband, which he constantly fails to pay.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0027 }

“Putting on those horrible stockings was simply more than I could endure. They possessed such an unattractive, coarse appearance and caused such an unpleasant, prickly sensation. Every single person would have mocked me. Initially, my intention was to feign an illness so I could miss going to church the following morning, yet I concluded that was impossible for me, as it amounted to living a falsehood, something our father instructed us never, ever to engage in following mother's passing. Performing a deceitful deed is fully as wicked as uttering a untruth, even if I am aware of certain individuals, in this very Glen, who practice such deceptions without appearing to experience the slightest remorse. Although I refrain from naming anyone, their identities are known to me, as well as to father.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0028 }

“After that, I made every effort to contract a cold and become truly ill by placing my unclad feet on the snowbank located in the Methodist cemetery until Tobias dragged me away. Nevertheless, it failed to harm me in the least, meaning I was unable to avoid attending church. Consequently, I simply made up my mind to slip on my boots and attend in that manner. I am unable to understand why it was such a terrible thing, especially since I took great care to scrub my legs until they were as spotless as my face, yet, in any case, my father should not be held responsible for what happened. He was inside the study reflecting on his sermon along with other divine matters, and I stayed out of his sight prior to leaving for Sunday School. Father avoids staring at the legs of congregation members during services, which naturally meant he failed to observe mine, whereas every gossip took notice and gossiped about the matter, and that reason explains my decision to write this letter to the Journal as a way of clarifying things. I imagine my actions were extremely improper, given that everyone claims they were, and I feel remorse and am donning those terrible stockings as a form of self-punishment, even though father purchased two pleasant new black pairs for me immediately after Mr. Flagg’s store commenced business on Monday morning. However, the blame rests entirely on me, and should anyone fault father regarding the incident once they have perused this, they lack Christian virtues and thus their remarks do not bother me.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0029 }

“I wish to clarify one more matter before I finish speaking. Mary Stubbs mentioned to me that Mr. Evan Garrick believes the Lew Baxters stole potatoes from his field this past autumn. His potatoes were not touched by them. Although they are extremely poor, they possess honesty. We were the ones responsible—Tobias, Rupert, and myself. Ida was absent from our group when it happened. It never crossed our minds that this was theft. Our only desire was a handful of potatoes to roast over a Fern Hollow campfire one night, accompanying the trout we fried. Situated right between the valley and the village, Mr. Garrick’s field happened to be closest, so we scaled his fence and uprooted several plants. Because Mr. Garrick failed to apply a sufficient amount of fertilizer, those potatoes were terribly tiny, forcing us to uproot numerous stalks to gather a decent quantity, and even then, their size barely surpassed marbles. Edmund and Izzy Carrow assisted us in consuming them, but their arrival occurred only after the cooking was finished, and they lacked any knowledge of our source, meaning they bear no fault whatsoever, only the three of us do. Harm was not our intention, yet should this count as stealing, our regrets are deep, and we shall reimburse Mr. Garrick for the crop if he allows us time to reach adulthood. At present, we possess no funds since our age prevents us from earning any, and Aunt Martha claims that maintaining this home consumes every single penny of poor father’s income, even on the rare occasions when it arrives on time. Nevertheless, Mr. Garrick has to stop accusing the Lew Baxters, who were completely faultless, and ruining their reputation.
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0030 }

“With respect, “GRACE ASHDOWN.”
{: #nw-v05-c25-p0031 }
